clinical: Without enough iron the marrow makes too little haemoglobin, so red cells become small and pale (microcytic and hypochromic), with a wider central pallor on a blood smear.
A platelet count below the normal range of about 150,000 to 400,000/mm3 (thrombocytopenia) tends to cause easy bruising and bleeding, mostly from the skin and mucous membranes.

Granulocytes.description: Granulocytes are white blood cells whose cytoplasm holds visible granules: neutrophils, the most common, which engulf and destroy bacteria; eosinophils, which fight parasites and drive allergic reactions; and basophils, the rarest, which release histamine in allergy. Their nuclei are lobed, which helps tell them apart from the round-nucleated lymphocytes.
clinical: A neutrophil count below about 1,500/mm3 (neutropenia) leaves the body vulnerable to serious bacterial infection, and the risk rises as the count falls.
A high eosinophil count is typical of parasitic worm infections and of allergic disorders such as asthma.

Agranulocytes.description: Agranulocytes are white blood cells without the conspicuous granules of granulocytes. Lymphocytes in this group include T cells and B cells, which drive the adaptive immune response, and natural killer cells, which destroy virus-infected and tumour cells. Monocytes, the largest white blood cells, become macrophages once they leave the blood for the tissues.
clinical: Infectious mononucleosis, most often caused by Epstein-Barr virus, produces a large rise in atypical lymphocytes, which are large, activated T cells.
Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is a cancer in which clonal B lymphocytes that look like small lymphocytes accumulate in the blood, marrow and lymph nodes.
A clot that forms inside an intact vessel is a thrombosis; in a deep leg vein it causes deep vein thrombosis, and a fragment that breaks off and lodges in the lungs causes a pulmonary embolism.
In haemophilia, a missing clotting factor (VIII or IX) means too little thrombin is generated to convert fibrinogen into fibrin, so clots form slowly and bleeding lasts longer.

Plasma.description: Plasma is the straw-coloured liquid that makes up about 55% of blood volume and carries the blood cells and platelets. It is mostly water, with dissolved proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones and waste products.
clinical: Low plasma albumin (hypoalbuminaemia), seen in liver disease, nephrotic syndrome and malnutrition, weakens the osmotic pull that keeps fluid inside vessels, so fluid leaks into the tissues as oedema.

parts.description: Erythrocytes (red blood cells) are biconcave discs, about 7.5 um across, with no nucleus (anucleate), that carry oxygen bound to haemoglobin. Their shape gives a large surface for gas exchange and lets them squeeze through capillaries narrower than themselves. On a stained smear they look pink with a pale central area (central pallor), because the centre is thinner than the rim.

Rouleau (plural rouleaux) is a stack of red cells lying face to face, like a pile of coins. Small rouleaux form in thick areas of any blood smear, but extensive rouleaux form when large plasma proteins such as fibrinogen and immunoglobulins reduce the negative surface charge (zeta potential) that normally keeps red cells apart. This happens in inflammation and pregnancy, and most strikingly in multiple myeloma. Rouleaux settle quickly, which is the basis of the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) test.

Platelets (thrombocytes) are small fragments without a nucleus, shed from megakaryocytes (large marrow cells that make them), and are about 2-4 um across. Normal counts are 150,000-400,000/mm3, and on a smear they look like small purple granular discs, often in clumps, with a granular centre and a pale blue rim. They plug breaches in damaged vessel walls and provide the surface on which clotting reactions occur. A low count (thrombocytopenia) causes pinpoint skin bleeds called petechiae and easy bruising.

The neutrophil nucleus is the dark purple, multi-lobed nucleus of a mature neutrophil, usually divided into three to five lobes joined by thin strands of chromatin (the DNA and protein packed in the nucleus). The lobed shape gives the cell its alternative name, polymorphonuclear (many-shaped nucleus), and it is the main feature used to tell a mature neutrophil from a band form. In a band neutrophil the nucleus is instead one continuous, curved, unsegmented bar.

Neutrophil granules are the fine, pale lilac-pink granules filling the cytoplasm; they take up neither the acidic nor the basic dye strongly, which is why the cell is called 'neutrophilic'. Primary (azurophilic) granules are lysosomes containing myeloperoxidase, elastase and defensins, while the more numerous secondary (specific) granules hold lactoferrin, lysozyme and collagenase, which help to kill microbes and clear damaged tissue. In severe infection, coarse dark 'toxic granulation' can appear.

The eosinophil nucleus is usually bilobed, with two rounded lobes joined by a thin strand, giving a 'spectacles' or 'telephone receiver' appearance. It is typically paler and less dense than a neutrophil's nucleus. Together with the bright orange-red granules filling the cytoplasm, this two-lobed shape is the main clue for recognising an eosinophil on a stained smear.

Eosinophil granules are large (about 0.5-1 um), round and refractile (they look shiny under the microscope), and stain bright orange-red with the acidic dye eosin. Each granule has a crystalline core of major basic protein surrounded by eosinophil cationic protein, eosinophil peroxidase and eosinophil-derived neurotoxin, which are toxic to parasitic worms and can also damage the host's own tissue. They are important both in defence against parasites and in the tissue damage seen in asthma.

Basophils are the rarest white blood cells, at about 0.5-1% of the total. Their bilobed or S-shaped nucleus is largely hidden by coarse, dark blue-purple granules containing histamine, which dilates vessels and makes capillaries leaky, and heparin, an anticoagulant. Each basophil carries surface IgE receptors, so when allergen cross-links IgE on the cell, the granules are released and drive allergic reactions.

The basophil nucleus is S-shaped or bilobed and paler than a neutrophil's nucleus. On a stained smear it is usually partly hidden by the dense cytoplasmic granules, so the cell is identified by the pale, lobed outline showing through them.

Basophil granules are large, uneven, deep blue-purple granules that fill much of the cytoplasm. They stain with basic dyes (basophilic) because they contain sulphated heparin, and they show metachromasia, a change in the dye's colour toward purple. The granules hold histamine, heparin and chemotactic factors (signals that attract other white cells), which are released when allergen cross-links the IgE on the cell surface.

T lymphocytes are small lymphocytes, about the size of a red cell, that mature in the thymus and form the cell-mediated arm of the immune system. Cytotoxic (CD8-positive) T cells kill virus-infected and tumour cells, while helper (CD4-positive) T cells direct other immune responses. They look like any small lymphocyte on a stained smear, with a round, dense dark purple nucleus and a thin rim of sky-blue cytoplasm, so CD3 with CD4 or CD8 surface markers is needed to confirm the type.

B lymphocytes are small lymphocytes that mature in the bone marrow and, once activated, turn into plasma cells that secrete antibody (humoral immunity). Their surface carries membrane-bound immunoglobulin, the B-cell antigen receptor, which binds native antigen directly. Like T lymphocytes they look identical on a stained smear, so the type is confirmed with surface markers such as CD19 or CD20.

Large lymphocytes are noticeably bigger than small lymphocytes, with more pale blue cytoplasm and a relatively eccentric (off-centre), round nucleus. They include activated lymphocytes and natural killer (NK) cells, which kill virus-infected and tumour cells without needing prior exposure to the antigen. Size alone does not show whether a cell is activated or is an NK cell, although some large granular lymphocytes contain azurophilic (purple-staining) granules.

The T lymphocyte nucleus is round or slightly indented, with dense, coarsely clumped dark purple chromatin (packed DNA) that fills most of the small cell. Its width is roughly that of a red cell, which makes it a handy size yardstick on a smear. On routine stains it looks the same as a B lymphocyte nucleus, so the cell cannot be typed from its nucleus alone.

The B lymphocyte nucleus is round or slightly indented, with dense, coarsely clumped dark chromatin (packed DNA) that fills most of the small cell and leaves only a thin rim of cytoplasm. Its width is roughly that of a red cell, but on an ordinary stain its nucleus cannot be told from a T lymphocyte nucleus.

The large lymphocyte nucleus is round or slightly indented and set off-centre in a larger cell, with less densely clumped chromatin than a small lymphocyte's. The paler, more open chromatin, together with the broader rim of pale blue cytoplasm around it, helps separate a large lymphocyte from a small one on a smear.

The T-cell receptor (TCR) is the antigen-recognising molecule on the surface of T lymphocytes. It is made of an alpha-beta chain pair (a gamma-delta pair in a small minority of T cells) linked to the CD3 signalling complex, and it recognises short peptide fragments displayed by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules on other cells. Being a molecule, it cannot be seen on an ordinary blood smear; it is detected by flow cytometry or immunostaining with anti-TCR antibodies, while CD3, present on all T cells, is used to identify them.

B-cell surface immunoglobulin is the membrane-bound form of antibody that acts as the B-cell antigen receptor, mostly IgM and IgD on naive (unexposed) B cells. It binds native, unprocessed antigen directly, and this binding can trigger the B cell to divide and differentiate. Unlike the soluble antibody secreted by plasma cells, it is anchored in the cell membrane, so it cannot be seen as a separate molecule on an ordinary smear.

Monocytes are the largest white blood cells, about 12-20 um, making up roughly 3-8% of white cells. They have abundant grey-blue, 'ground glass' cytoplasm, often with small vacuoles, around a large kidney- or horseshoe-shaped nucleus with lacy, less condensed chromatin. Monocytes leave the blood and mature into tissue macrophages, which engulf microbes and debris and present antigen to lymphocytes.

The monocyte nucleus is large, eccentric (set to one side), and kidney-bean or horseshoe shaped. Its chromatin is delicate and lacy, and it stains paler than a lymphocyte's. These two features, the shape and the open chromatin, are what separate a monocyte from a large lymphocyte on a smear.

Fibrin is the insoluble protein that forms the mesh of a blood clot. Thrombin cuts soluble fibrinogen, a plasma protein made by the liver, into fibrin monomers that polymerise into long strands, which are then cross-linked by activated factor XIII. The mesh traps red cells and platelets to form a stable clot, and plasmin later dissolves it, releasing D-dimers as breakdown products.
